Decode an allergy score into the allergens it includes.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/allergies) (MIT). Listed under [Numbers & Math](/examples/?subject=numbers-and-math).

```nomi-run
// FILE: allergies.nomi
/// The allergens a score covers, in score order: eggs are worth 1, peanuts 2,
/// and each one after twice the one before.
pub enum Allergen {
    Eggs
    Peanuts
    Shellfish
    Strawberries
    Tomatoes
    Chocolate
    Pollen
    Cats
}

derive Variants for Allergen

/// Reports whether `score` includes `allergen`.
pub fn allergic_to?(score: Int, allergen: Allergen) -> Bool {
    Int.bitwise_and(score, value(allergen)) != 0
}

/// Lists every allergen `score` includes, in score order. Parts of the score
/// above the last allergen are ignored.
pub fn list(score: Int) -> List<Allergen> {
    Allergen.variants()
    |> Iter.filter(&allergic_to?(score, &1))
    |> Iter.to_list()
}

fn value(allergen: Allergen) -> Int {
    case allergen {
        .Eggs -> 1
        .Peanuts -> 2
        .Shellfish -> 4
        .Strawberries -> 8
        .Tomatoes -> 16
        .Chocolate -> 32
        .Pollen -> 64
        .Cats -> 128
    }
}

// FILE: allergies_test.nomi
import {
    allergies
    allergies.Allergen
}

test "testing for eggs allergy" {
    cases = [
        #("not allergic to anything", 0, False),
        #("allergic only to eggs", 1, True),
        #("allergic to eggs and something else", 3, True),
        #("allergic to something, but not eggs", 2, False),
        #("allergic to everything", 255, True),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, score, expected), description {
        assert allergies.allergic_to?(score, Allergen.Eggs) == expected
    }
}

test "list when:" {
    cases: List<#(String, Int, List<Allergen>)> = [
        #("no allergies", 0, []),
        #("just eggs", 1, [.Eggs]),
        #("just peanuts", 2, [.Peanuts]),
        #("just strawberries", 8, [.Strawberries]),
        #("eggs and peanuts", 3, [.Eggs, .Peanuts]),
        #("more than eggs but not peanuts", 5, [.Eggs, .Shellfish]),
        #("lots of stuff", 248, [.Strawberries, .Tomatoes, .Chocolate, .Pollen, .Cats]),
        #(
            "everything",
            255,
            [.Eggs, .Peanuts, .Shellfish, .Strawberries, .Tomatoes, .Chocolate, .Pollen, .Cats],
        ),
        #(
            "no allergen score parts",
            509,
            [.Eggs, .Shellfish, .Strawberries, .Tomatoes, .Chocolate, .Pollen, .Cats],
        ),
        #("no allergen score parts without highest valid score", 257, [.Eggs]),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, score, expected), description {
        assert allergies.list(score) == expected
    }
}
```

## How it's written

- Allergens are an enum, and `derive Variants` gives `Allergen.variants()` in declaration order, which is the score order `list` must answer in.
- Each allergen's score is spelled out in a `case` (`value`), rather than computed as `Int.shift_left(1, index)` from its position in `variants()`. The table is the problem statement, and reordering the enum cannot silently change it.
- `allergic_to?` takes the score first, so `list` reads `Iter.filter(&allergic_to?(score, &1))`, a capture (style §31).
- The canonical `item` strings become variants in the tests (`Allergen.Eggs`); there is no string parsing in the API.
- The `list` table needs its type written out (`List<#(String, Int, List<Allergen>)>`), because `.Eggs` inside an unannotated list literal has no enum to resolve against.
